analysis.one_liner: Lets the FTC impose civil penalties on COVID-19 scams, including fake cures and benefit fraud.
analysis.headline: Introduced with support from both parties in December 2020, the bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received any further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 public health emergency, this bill would make it unlawful to run deceptive schemes connected to COVID-19 treatments, cures, prevention, diagnosis, or related government benefits. It gives the Federal Trade Commission the power to seek civil penalties against violators, on top of its existing authority to stop deceptive ads and sales pitches. The bill was introduced in the Senate days before the congressional session ended and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers targeted by pandemic-era scams — people sold fake COVID-19 cures or testing, or tricked out of government benefits like stimulus payments — would gain a stronger enforcement tool, because companies could face civil fines, not just orders to stop advertising.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to engage in deceptive practices tied to the treatment, cure, prevention, mitigation, or diagnosis of COVID-19, or to COVID-19-related government benefits, for the duration of the declared public health emergency.

Treats violations as breaches of an FTC trade rule, so the FTC can enforce them with the same powers it uses under its own statute, including civil penalties, while preserving all of its other authority.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and individuals running deceptive COVID-related schemes would bear civil penalties. Legitimate companies are only exposed if they engage in deception, which is already unlawful under the FTC Act.

drawbacks.text: The prohibition applies only to COVID-19-related deception and only for the duration of the declared public health emergency, so it leaves similar scams about other products or emergencies uncovered.

The FTC already has authority to pursue deceptive practices under section 5 of the FTC Act; the bill's main addition is easier access to civil penalties, a targeted but incremental change rather than a new enforcement regime.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is narrow but well-aimed: it adds a real deterrent (civil fines) against pandemic fraud that cost consumers money and endangered health, and its cost falls almost entirely on bad-faith actors. Its main weakness is that it expires with the emergency declaration rather than strengthening consumer protection permanently.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 20, 2020, read twice, and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat with no hearings, no markup, and no vote before the session ended two weeks later.

narrative.text: Sen. Maria Cantwell introduced the bill on December 20, 2020, for herself and Sen. Roger Wicker, the top Republican on the Senate Commerce Committee.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced.
The bill's only action was that referral; no committee vote, floor debate, or roll call ever occurred, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

The bill would have authorized the FTC to seek civil penalties for deceptive practices associated with COVID-19 treatment, cure, prevention, mitigation, diagnosis, or related government benefits during the public health emergency.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of COVID-related scams are better off, since no new civil-penalty exposure was created; consumers were left with the FTC's existing, slower remedies for first-time violators.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: COVID scam operators and no one else

for.name: Sen. Maria Cantwell
for.role: U.S. Senator from Washington; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 20, 2020, authorizing FTC civil penalties against COVID-related deceptive practices.

for.name: Sen. Roger Wicker
for.role: U.S. Senator from Mississippi; original cosponsor and chairman of the Senate Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor of the bill, though the committee he chaired never took action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Democratic sponsor and its sole cosponsor was the Republican chairman of the committee it was referred to; it died with no recorded opposition and no votes.

industries.industry: Pandemic-era scam operators and fraudulent health-product marketers
industries.note: These businesses profit by selling fake cures, tests, or protections and by tricking people out of COVID-related government benefits; the bill would expose them to FTC civil penalties. Consumers bear the cost of these schemes today.
Legitimate marketers face new penalty exposure only for deceptive COVID claims, which is already illegal; honest firms bear essentially no new burden.
